newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Buy opposite ends of Finland, Sweden.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Buy opposite ends of Finland, Sweden.

text.p: The long end of Finland and the short end of Sweden offer the best chance for gains among Nordic bond markets as European bond convergence continues unabated, analysts said on Tuesday.
High-flying currencies in Finland and Sweden should give these northern markets added spice but interest rate concerns, particularly in Norway, may soon crop up.

"In Finland, there is biggest scope for further convergence," said Wike Groenenbergh, European economist at Salomon Brothers in London. "The 10-year bond spread should virtually disappear over the next six to nine months because it will be clear Finland will be joining a monetary union."
The gaps between 10-year Nordic and benchmark German Bunds have narrowed steadily amid unrelenting optimism over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Finland is seen as a strong candidate for EMU and although Sweden has ruled out participation in the first wave in 1999, it should nevertheless ride the convergence bandwagon, analysts said.

The Swedish crown has shot close to its highs for the year against the mark while the Finnish markka has reached its strongest level since February, as the German currency stumbles against the dollar and British pound.
The Norwegian crown has not fared so well, pulling off peaks earlier in the year and settling back into December 1996 ranges.

Groenenbergh said the Finnish market may suffer from the lack of liquidity across the curve but the gap between 10-year German and comparable Finnish yields should continue to evaporate from the current spread of around 30 basis points.
Data from Finland earlier on Tuesday may prompt concern about rising interest rates but Groenenbergh did not see it having too harsh an impact on the spread.

Finland reported core inflation rose 0.5 percent year-on-year in May compared with analysts' expectations of 0.4 percent. Industrial production rose 6.1 percent year-on-year in May compared with a 7.9 percent rise in April.

"There could be a rate rise...but I do not necessarily think it will lead to a significant widening on the long end," she said. "If Finland starts to hike, it's starting the cycle earlier than other countries."
Stephanie Pfeifer, European economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, did not see the Finnish central bank moving just yet.

"I think the central bank will be getting quite worried, especially about the construction sector," she said. "But I don't think they'll raise rates yet because the markka is strong against the mark. They might even wait for wage negotiations in the autumn."

Pfeifer however, favoured Sweden, forecasting the Swedish 10-year yield gap to narrow to around 80 basis points on a three-month view from 90 basis points now. Here too, the strong crown would give the more liquid Swedish bond market a lift.
"And I think it's still going to benefit if we see any further convergence in the rest of Europe," she said.
Groenenbergh however, saw value at the short end of Sweden, where markets are overplaying interest rate concerns.
"I believe the market should not be discounting any interest rate increase this year and up to 75 basis points or so in December 1998," she said.
The yield spread between two-year Swedish and German notes is around 110 basis points.

Pfeifer said speculation has increased that Norwegian interest rates may also be heading higher but she expected the central bank here to hold off as well, ahead of parliamentary elections in September.

"There was a lot of speculation on Friday they would hike the official rates because the fixed deposits have been creeping up," she said. "I think it's too soon there as well because the crown has strengthened a little bit."
Nevertheless she was not positive on Norwegian bonds.

James McKay, international economist at PaineWebber in London, was more pessimistic on the outlook for Nordic bonds. He saw recent convergence reaching the end of the line and the Sweden/German spread stretching to 115 basis points on a three-month view.
"I think we've seen about the best we're going to see at the longer end of the (Swedish) curve," he said. "I would recommend people shorten duration." -- International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
